questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: Governing by grant in the early Zhou
questions.learningObjective: explain how an early dynasty governed through grants to relatives and allies
questions.stem: An early Chinese dynasty ruled by granting land and a title to relatives and allies, who were expected in return to send military support and to observe the rituals of the court. What was the point of that arrangement?

options.text: It was meant to hold a very wide territory with a very small centre, so that control rested on obligations between families rather than on a permanent administration
It was meant to raise an army quickly, since allies who owed a duty were more reliable than soldiers who were paid
options.misconception: picks one of the arrangement's effects and calls it the purpose, when the arrangement was about ruling territory at all

options.text: It was meant to reward service, so that a grant was a payment for work already done rather than an exchange of duties for land
options.misconception: turns a standing obligation into a completed payment, which removes the continuing relationship the arrangement depended on

options.text: It was meant to keep the royal family together, so that the grants prevented any single branch from becoming strong enough to rival the centre
options.misconception: reverses the effect, since a grant made a branch strong and that strength is what later weakened the centre

questions.explanation: The arrangement is a response to a scale problem, and reading it that way explains the parts that otherwise look puzzling. A dynasty that has just unified a large region has far more territory than it can staff with officials it appoints, so it governs through people who are already related to the court or already allied with it: they hold the land, they keep the local order, and they supply troops and ritual observance when the centre calls for them. Control is therefore a matter of obligation between families, and it is cheap in the only sense that matters to a small court, which administers its own immediate surroundings and relies on others for the rest. The weakness is written into the design, and it is worth stating because it sets up everything that follows: each generation makes the grant more secure for the grantee and less secure for the centre, since the family that has held a state for three generations regards it as its own. By the time the arrangement has run for centuries the states are large, self-supporting and effectively independent, and the dynasty is nominally above a political map it no longer governs. The distractors each take one element for the whole. B isolates the military clause. C converts a continuing duty into a settled payment, which removes the obligation. D gets the direction of the effect exactly backwards, and it is the error a reader is most likely to make because the intuition that a centre wants weak relatives is right in general and wrong here.
questions.hint: Ask what problem a small court has when the territory is very large, and what the grant obliges the grantee to send.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: What a grant document obliges
questions.learningObjective: read a grant document for the obligation it creates rather than for the favour it records
questions.stem: A surviving grant of land records a recipient, a piece of territory, the population on it, and a list of the ritual vessels to be brought to the court on specified occasions. Which reading of the document is the soundest?

options.text: The document confers a right and states a price, so the interesting part is what the recipient must deliver for the land to remain his
The document is a receipt, so the fact that it names a price means the land was purchased rather than granted
options.misconception: reads a stated consideration as a commercial transaction, when the vessels are the performance of an obligation

options.text: The document is a legal instrument with no political content, so the ritual requirements show only that the court was interested in ceremony
options.misconception: treats obligation as decoration, when the ceremony is the enforceable part of the grant

options.text: The document proves the centre controlled the land directly, since only a ruler who administered it personally could write this
options.misconception: reads a grant as direct administration, which is the arrangement the grant exists to avoid

questions.explanation: A grant document is worth reading for the same reason a contract is: the interesting information is the obligation, and a reader who stops at the conferral has read the easy half. Here the recipient, the territory, the people on it and the vessels are all listed, and the last of these is the operative clause, because it names what has to be delivered and when. That converts the document from a favour into a standing relationship with a price attached, and it explains the two features that look like padding. A population is listed because people are part of what a territory contains and a ruler who grants land is thereby saying who is expected to work it; vessels are listed because specified objects arriving on specified occasions is a claim that can be checked by whether they arrive. A reader who has understood this can date and interpret a whole class of documents. The distractors each make the document something other than an obligation. B is the misreading that comes from translating the word for consideration as price, which is a genuine ambiguity in the language of gifts and one that a reader of later commercial documents will fall into. C mistakes the least decorative clause for the least important one. D reverses the arrangement entirely, and it is the error a reader is most likely to make, because a document that comes from a court does look like the voice of a ruler in person.
questions.hint: Ask which part of the list could be checked by whether something arrived on a certain day.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: Questions written on bone
questions.learningObjective: explain what the earliest substantial written corpus was used for
questions.stem: The oldest substantial body of Chinese writing that survives was cut into turtle shells and cattle shoulder blades, and most of the inscriptions are a question put to a spirit or an ancestor together with the answer that came back. What does that tell a reader about what writing was for?

options.text: It began as a way of putting a question to a power that had to be consulted, and a written record was needed because the answer mattered and the question had to be exact
It began as a way of keeping a government account, so a reader should expect these inscriptions to be a treasury list
options.misconception: assigns the corpus to a later function, when the inscriptions themselves name divination as their purpose

options.text: It began as decoration, since carved characters on valuable material were a display of learning before they were a record of anything
options.misconception: reverses the priority, since the content of these particular inscriptions is entirely practical

options.text: It began as a way of fixing a spoken promise, so the earliest writing should be read as an early form of contract
options.misconception: supplies a legal purpose the material gives no sign of

questions.explanation: The material answers the question on its own, and a reader who notices this has learned the method the whole subject rests on: the content of a document tells you what it was for. These inscriptions are queries and their answers, and the queries are about matters a court cannot decide by itself, which is why they go to a spirit: the coming rain, the outcome of war, the birth of a child, the right day for a journey. In that setting writing is not decoration and not administration; it is the technology of asking exactly, and exactness is the point, since a question put carelessly gets a meaningless answer and the person who carved it had to be able to write a date, a place, a number of cattle and a set of possible outcomes correctly. A reader should also be careful about the limits of the evidence, because the fact that the oldest substantial corpus is divinatory does not mean the earliest writing was; a corpus survives where the material and the climate allow, and the honest statement is that this is the oldest substantial body that has survived, not the first writing there ever was. The distractors each substitute a function the inscriptions do not claim. B assigns them to a treasury, C reads them as display, and D reads them as a legal form, and all three do it by ignoring what the objects say.
questions.hint: Read the content of the inscriptions rather than the material they are cut into, and ask what a query needs to be correct.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: What a survival bias does to a claim
questions.learningObjective: evaluate a claim about the past that rests on what has survived
questions.stem: A student concludes that because the earliest surviving writing is a set of divination records, early society was a society of divination. Which evaluation of that conclusion is the fairest?

options.text: The conclusion draws a claim about a whole society from the one kind of document that happens to have survived, and a set of preserved records is a set of records worth keeping
The conclusion is sound, because a society that wrote nothing but divination records cannot have done anything else worth recording
options.misconception: assumes that what was not written was not done, which is the assumption a reader must test rather than accept

options.text: The conclusion is unsound, because the divination records are the only evidence available and an argument from a single kind of evidence is never acceptable
options.misconception: rules out a whole class of reasoning rather than narrowing it, which would leave almost no claim about the past makeable

options.text: The conclusion is unsound, because writing of that kind was in fact only used for record-keeping and the divination reading comes from a later interpretation
options.misconception: invents a different content for the corpus, when the inscriptions name the spirits they address

questions.explanation: The student has made a general claim out of a restricted sample, and the restriction is not a fact about the past but a fact about what has survived. A corpus comes down to us for reasons that have nothing to do with how common the practice was: bone, bronze, bamboo and paper differ enormously in how well they last, and institutions, ritual and the wealthy produce records while ordinary transactions produce few. What a reader has is therefore doubly selected, first by the people who chose to write things down and then by the ground that kept them, and neither selection is neutral. The correct response is not to throw the evidence away but to size the claim to it: these inscriptions establish that divination was practised and was thought to require exact wording, and they say very little about how much of ordinary life it occupied. That is a stronger and more useful conclusion than either the student's or a refusal to reason at all. The distractors each fail differently. B asserts the assumption directly, which is the error. C is the overcorrection, and it is a common and damaging one, because refusing to argue from a restricted corpus does not produce caution, it produces silence. D is the most confident of the three and the least supported, since it asserts a different content for material the reader has not examined.
questions.hint: Ask why these particular documents survived, and what that says about the society as opposed to the archive.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: What the examinations changed
questions.learningObjective: state the social effect an examination system had over centuries
questions.stem: For most of Chinese history an appointment to office was reached by an examination on the Confucian classics. Which of the following is the effect that belongs to that arrangement?

options.text: It gave a route into office that did not depend on birth, and over centuries that route came to matter more than family connection
It produced an administration of unrivalled competence, since a person who passed an examination was necessarily the best person available
options.misconception: reads a competitive test as a complete measure of ability, and it tests one kind of learning very well

options.text: It ended hereditary privilege at once, so a family could not hold office for more than one generation
options.misconception: overstates the speed of the change, when the system and established families coexisted for a very long time

options.text: It was open to everybody, since nothing in the examinations required literacy and a candidate needed no preparation
options.misconception: denies the literacy the examinations assumed, and preparation is precisely what families with means could supply

questions.explanation: The important effect is a change in who could claim office, and it is worth stating the mechanism as well as the result. A competitive examination on a fixed body of texts creates a test that is in principle open to any prepared candidate, and the text being fixed is what makes it comparable: two men from different provinces answering the same question can be ranked by the same standard. Over a long period that standard strengthened against the older channels of family connection, and the result was a governing elite defined by shared learning rather than by descent. The point to hold onto is the timescale: this took centuries, and the system coexisted with powerful families for most of that time, which is why a claim of instant meritocracy is wrong and a claim of a real and growing alternative is right. The study of this arrangement also has to be done with two further cautions, because they are what a good answer is expected to add. It did not cover every post; military, technical and many local posts were filled by other routes. And a test of classical learning measures one kind of capacity, so a system resting on it shaped what the elite read and argued about. The distractors each overreach. B turns a test into a proof of ability. C accelerates a slow change into an instant one. D denies the literacy the whole design assumes, and that denial is what produces the belief that the system was socially neutral when it plainly was not.
questions.hint: Ask what a fixed text and a common test make possible, and over what period the change actually worked.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: Reading an examination claim
questions.learningObjective: explain what a merit-based claim about an old institution does and does not follow from the evidence
questions.stem: Explain in your own words what would have to be true for an old competitive examination to count as an equal route into office, and say which of those conditions held and which did not.

answer.exemplar: An examination system counts as an equal route only if four things are separately true, and a good answer says which of them were true rather than treating the whole question as one thing. The first is that the test is genuinely competitive, meaning that the number of places is limited and the standard is applied to every candidate. That held, and it is why the system is remarkable in its own terms rather than a formality. The second is that the standard is the same for everyone who takes it, which is the property the fixed body of classical texts supplies: two candidates from distant provinces answering the same question can be ranked against the same criterion. That held too, and it is a stronger point than the first. The third is that no candidate needs resources a poor family cannot supply. This did not hold, and the reason is worth tracing rather than merely noting, because preparation meant years of study with no income, books, and a teacher, and those are things a family with means buys. The fourth is that passing opened office rather than a better position in the queue. That held only partly: the examination created a route, and it did so over a very long period during which powerful families used the route their families had already had. So the honest summary is that the arrangement genuinely opened a door that had been narrower before, and that it did so alongside families who kept the advantage they had. The common error is to describe it in one word in either direction, and the cost of that word is that it prevents the reader from seeing the change. A system can be both an opening and a reinforcement of privilege at the same time, and this one was, for as long as the two channels ran in parallel. The general lesson is that a question about an old institution should be decomposed into the conditions it would require, checked one at a time against what the records show, and answered with a mixture rather than with a verdict.

questions.explanation: The exemplar is marked correct for decomposing merit into separately checkable conditions, for identifying the resource requirement as the condition that failed rather than as a vague unfairness, and for concluding with a mixture rather than a verdict. A response that says the system was meritocratic has asserted a word instead of checking a set of conditions.
questions.hint: Ask what an equal route would require, and check each requirement against what a poor family could supply.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: What a unification has to settle
questions.learningObjective: select the measures a unification required in order to hold together what it had conquered
questions.stem: A first empire has conquered several states and taken their territory in one stroke. Four of the five measures below are ones such a conquest makes necessary. Which four?

options.text: A single form of writing, so that an order issued at the centre can be read in a territory where the old scripts differ
Common measures of weight and length, so that a quantity taxed in one place means the same quantity in the next
One standard width for cart wheels, so that vehicles can pass a gate and a road built for another state
A single set of coinage, so that a tax paid in one province is not refused in the next
One official written history of the period, so that the new state is described in a single approved account
options.misconception: promotes a later scholarly genre into a founding necessity, when a conquest has an immediate practical problem that this does not meet

questions.explanation: The four measures in the keyed set share one property: each removes a friction that conquest creates and does not remove by itself. A newly conquered territory is added to an existing state, and the people of that state keep the weights, the lengths, the coins and the writing they were used to, so a centre that does not standardise them is governing a single political unit with several commercial ones. That is why the first measure is script: an order that cannot be read is not an order, and a tax assessed in a unit the taxpayer does not use is an assessment that produces an argument. The cart width is the item learners forget and it is the most concrete of the five, because it is a measurement with a physical consequence: a wheel gauge fixes the width of a rut, and a rut fixes the axle, and a road or a gateway built for a different gauge is a wall. Coinage is the one a reader meets daily, and the reason for standardising it is the same in a sharper form, since a tax receipt in a coin the next province will not accept is not a receipt. The fifth item is the one to reject, and the error it names is the confusion of a founding measure with a later genre. Official histories do exist and do matter enormously, but they answer a question about how a regime is remembered, and the problem in front of the new state is whether an order can be obeyed.
questions.hint: Apply one test to each: does the friction exist the moment the conquest is finished, and does it stop a command or a payment?

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: The cost of standardising a script
questions.learningObjective: explain what a script standardisation achieved and what it cost
questions.stem: After a conquest the new government ordered a single official script for use in government and required the old ones to be abandoned. Which statement about that order is the fairest?

options.text: It solved the problem of an order nobody could read and it made a large number of existing documents unreadable to the people who had written them
It succeeded completely, so a reader who finds a pre-conquest text today will have no difficulty with it
options.misconception: assumes a policy was fully implemented in a generation, which is a claim about compliance rather than about the policy

options.text: It was a mistake, because a state has no business deciding how its subjects write
options.misconception: argues from a later intuition about writing while ignoring the administrative problem the order was solving

options.text: It mainly served to keep one family in power, since a shared script is always a way of restricting who can read government
options.misconception: supplies a motive that the measure does not require, since the effect on literacy cuts the other way

questions.explanation: The order is a good example of a policy whose benefit and its cost are the same fact seen from two sides, and a reader who wants to judge it has to hold both. The benefit is administrative and immediate: a centre that has just taken several territories cannot govern them if its orders arrive in a script the recipients cannot read, and a script standardisation is the cheapest way to make one state out of several. The cost falls on knowledge rather than on people, and it is worth being precise about that, because the loss is not that anything was destroyed but that a large body of earlier writing became inaccessible to ordinary readers, including records of land, contracts, ritual and family descent that had real value to the people who owned them. That is a genuine loss, and it is also the reason the study of early texts is hard, so the two facts are the same fact. What the order did not do is make the old writing disappear, which is a point that protects against two symmetrical errors: the claim that it succeeded completely, and the claim that it destroyed the record. The distractors each take one side. B assumes a policy took effect in a generation, which is a claim about how people obeyed and not about what the policy was. C argues from a later intuition about writing while ignoring the problem being solved. D is the interesting one, because restricting who can read a script is a real possibility in general, and here the effect runs the other way, since literacy among ordinary people is exactly what a single simple script encourages.
questions.hint: Ask what the order fixed and what it made harder to reach, and notice that these are two descriptions of one change.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: How a frontier was pushed outward
questions.learningObjective: identify the methods by which a dynasty extended its frontier
questions.stem: A dynasty spends a century pushing its border far to the north against a nomadic power. Which description fits the way that was actually done?

options.text: Campaigns and negotiated alliances used alternately, and the line moved further each time the fighting went badly for the nomads
A single continuous war, because a frontier can only be moved by force and never by agreement
options.misconception: turns one of the two methods into the only method, and the record contains the other

options.text: Trade agreements alone, since a dynasty that wanted the border moved would buy it with goods rather than take it
options.misconception: removes the fighting from a century of campaigning, which is the part the record is clearest about

options.text: Settlement by migration, since the dynasty moved its own people north and the border followed the people
options.misconception: confuses frontier defence with frontier settlement, which are different policies with different purposes

questions.explanation: The two methods appear together in the record, and their alternation is not a change of policy but the method itself, because the two are aimed at different situations. When the dynasty is in a strong position it campaigns, and the effect of a successful campaign is that the nomads withdraw and a line of garrisons and agreements is established behind them. When it is not, it negotiates, accepting a smaller line in exchange for peace and a supply of goods. What makes the frontier move over a century is the pattern of those alternations, and a reader should note that the two methods are not moral opposites: a negotiated line is often the one that lasts, because a line drawn by a treaty is one the other party has agreed to. The reason this item matters beyond the fact is that the combination makes a simple claim of either kind wrong. A dynasty that fought and never negotiated appears aggressive and exhausting; a dynasty that only negotiated appears to have bought territory with goods, which is a different claim and a less likely one. The distractors each remove one half. B keeps the fighting and denies the treaties, C keeps the treaties and denies the fighting, and D substitutes settlement for expansion, which is a policy with a different aim: putting your own people in the frontier is a way of holding a line, not of pushing it outward.
questions.hint: Ask which two things a court does when it is strong and when it is not, and over which of them the frontier actually moved.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: What a claim of expansion rests on
questions.learningObjective: explain the evidence a claim of territorial expansion requires
questions.stem: Explain in your own words what a claim that a dynasty expanded its territory has to establish, and why a longer frontier is not by itself evidence that more land was held.

answer.exemplar: A claim about territory is a claim about control, and a longer line is a measurement of distance rather than of control, so the two have to be kept apart. What the claim has to establish is three things in a fixed order. First, that the line moved: that there was a border in one period and a different border in a later one, which is a comparison between two dated records and is the easiest of the three. Second, that the new line was actually held, by a garrison, an official, a tax office or an administration, rather than being announced and then abandoned; a claim resting on a proclamation establishes a policy, not a province. Third, that holding it was durable, which means the line survived the death of the commander who drew it, and this is the test that separates an expansion from a raid. Every one of those can fail independently, and the commonest failure in popular accounts is the first being mistaken for all three. A general who marches north and a general who marches north and leaves a governor behind have both extended a line, and only the second has extended a state. Why distance is not evidence is the general point rather than a detail of this case. A border drawn by treaty can be long and meaningless, because a treaty line records what two parties agreed on paper at a moment when neither could enforce it. A frontier defended by a moving column can be short and real, because the column is where the state's reach actually stops. So a reader should ask what stood on the other side of the line, not how far away it was, and should treat a figure of miles as a fact about geography and a fact about the records, neither of which is automatically a fact about power. The wider lesson is that territorial claims are the easiest kind of historical claim to state and the hardest to support, precisely because everyone repeats them.

questions.explanation: The exemplar is marked correct for separating a moved line from a held line, for requiring durability as a third condition rather than treating a proclamation as control, and for the general point that a figure of distance measures geography and not power. A response that says a longer frontier means more territory has confused the measurement with the claim.
questions.hint: Ask what stood on the far side of the line, and whether it was still there a decade later.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: What a tribute mission carried
questions.learningObjective: describe the exchange that stood behind the tribute system
questions.stem: Envoys from surrounding states travelled to the imperial court with tribute, and were received with gifts, ceremonies and permission to trade. What is the best description of what the arrangement was?

options.text: A standing framework in which the visiting side gave a gift in order to be recognised as a neighbour in good standing, and the receiving side gave goods and access in return
A tax system, since the goods handed over at the court were the price of the land the visitors occupied
options.misconception: reads a diplomatic gift as a fiscal claim, which changes the relation between the two sides entirely

options.text: A military alliance, since only a state that had submitted would be allowed to send an embassy at all
options.misconception: confuses recognition with military alignment, which the arrangement did not require

options.text: A closed system, since a state outside it was by definition outside the world of trade and could not obtain any goods at all
options.misconception: assumes a diplomatic boundary was a commercial one, and it emphatically was not

questions.explanation: The tribute framework is one of the most misdescribed arrangements in the history of the subject, and the reason is that the word tribute suggests extraction. What it was is a standing set of relations in which the smaller party came, brought a gift, and was recognised, and the larger party received it, returned a gift, and allowed the visitors to trade. Both sides gained something different: the visitors gained standing and access, the court gained acknowledgement of its position and the goods that came with the mission, and the trade that followed the embassy was real and often more valuable than the gift. The word for a tribute gift in this setting means a present, and a reader who hears tribute and reaches for tax has misread the whole system. Three features are worth adding because they explain the shape of the evidence. Missions were regular, so a court receives them in a rhythm and the record accumulates. Names and titles are negotiated in them, so the record is a source about relative standing. And the exchange runs both ways, since the returning ships and caravans carry the court's goods outward, which is why foreign observers who came for the tribute and stayed for the trade described the arrangement as commercial without being wrong. The distractors each make it something with more force in it. B turns a gift into a payment and makes the smaller party a tenant. C turns recognition into alliance. D is the error that is most worth correcting, because it treats a diplomatic ring as a wall, and it is the belief behind a long-standing claim that trade was cut off.
questions.hint: Ask what each side received, and whether a state outside the framework could still buy goods.

questions.topic: Reading a court record of a tribute mission
questions.learningObjective: draw an inference from a court record while marking the record's interest
questions.stem: A court record describes a mission from a northern state, lists the gifts that were presented, and records the ruler's title the visitors were granted. Which inference is best supported by that record?

options.text: The court claimed the northern ruler as a subordinate, and the record is written to preserve that claim, so the entry is evidence about the court's position
The northern ruler accepted the court's position without reservation, since a granted title is a title the visitor agreed to
options.misconception: reads a record of what the court granted as a record of what the other side accepted

options.text: The northern ruler considered himself the superior party, since the record describes a mission arriving rather than a court being visited
options.misconception: reads an absence of reciprocal visits as a claim of precedence the record does not make

options.text: The mission was a commercial enterprise, since the record lists the gifts in detail and a diplomatic visit would not bother with quantities
options.misconception: infers a commercial purpose from a court's interest in recording the value of what it received

questions.explanation: The record is a court document with a court's purposes, and the two entries a reader should notice are the ones doing the political work. The list of gifts is valuable to the court because it quantifies what the mission was worth, and it is also the entry that makes the record look most objective. The title is the entry that carries the claim, because in this framework a title granted by the court was a statement about standing, and the court had every reason to record the title it had granted rather than the title the visitor preferred. So the record is strong evidence about the relationship as the court described it, and weak evidence about the relationship as the other side understood it. That asymmetry is the general lesson and it is worth stating as a habit: when a record from a court survives, ask what the court wanted the record to establish. The distractors each make the mistake in a different direction. B reads a grant as an agreement, which is the classic error with a document that reports one party's act. C is interesting, and it is the objection a careful reader should raise, but it is raised from a silence rather than from anything the record says. D is the inference from detail, and it is instructive because detail is not evidence of a commercial purpose; a court is meticulous about value for its own reasons.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two entries is doing political work, and what the recording court wanted the document to establish.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: Why a long voyage could sail at all
questions.learningObjective: identify the technical basis of a long early fifteenth-century voyage
questions.stem: Early in the fifteenth century an enormous fleet travelled far across the sea to several states, carrying envoys, soldiers and goods, and returned years later. Which set of conditions made a voyage of that kind possible?

options.text: A compass for direction, a stern-mounted rudder for steerage in a heavy sea, and settled knowledge of when the seasonal winds reversed
A written agreement with the states visited, which allowed the fleet to use their harbours and resupply without asking
options.misconception: supplies a diplomatic arrangement for what the record shows was a technical problem the fleet solved itself

options.text: A merchant fleet that was already sailing those routes, which the expedition simply joined at sea
options.misconception: assumes a commercial route already existed, when the voyage was state-financed and diplomatic

options.text: A favourable season lasting the whole voyage, so that the fleet never met a contrary wind on the way out or back
options.misconception: removes the navigation problem, when the fleet planned its departures around winds that reversed on a known calendar

questions.explanation: The three conditions in the keyed answer are the ones that make a long sea voyage an operation rather than an accident, and each answers a different problem. Direction is the first: without knowing which way is north when there is no land in sight, a fleet cannot navigate at all, and the magnetic compass is the device that makes that possible on open water. Steerage is the second, and it is the least obvious of the three to a reader who has only thought of ships as moved by oars or by wind alone; a stern-mounted rudder lets a large vessel be held on a heading against wind and current, which is what makes a fleet of very large ships controllable. Winds are the third, and it is the one that turns a voyage into a plan: the seasonal reversal of the monsoon meant there were fixed windows in which a ship could go out and others in which it could come back, so a competent commander was not sailing optimistically but waiting for a date. The voyage's purpose also belongs in the answer to any question about it, because it explains the size: a fleet carrying envoys and troops to several states in turn is a diplomatic instrument, and it was financed and commanded as one. The distractors each supply an easier cause. B makes the technology into a treaty. C assumes the route was already being used. D is the appealing one, because a voyage that never met a contrary wind would be a different kind of story, and it removes the very problem the monsoon knowledge solves.
questions.hint: Ask what a commander needs to know when there is no land in sight, and when the winds will turn round.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: What a voyage record does not say
questions.learningObjective: identify the limits of a record written to celebrate a voyage
questions.stem: The official account of a great fifteenth-century fleet describes the size of the ships, the ranks of the officers, the gifts exchanged, and the magnificence of the reception at each port, and says nothing about the crews. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.text: The account is a record of what the expedition was for, since it is organised around the fleet's size, its rank and its generosity, and those are the categories of a diplomatic mission
The account shows the voyage was a commercial enterprise, since a trading record would be expected to list goods and would not list ranks
options.misconception: reads the listing of goods as evidence of trade, when a diplomatic gift is also goods and the ranks are the tell

options.text: The crews were unimportant, so their absence shows that the voyage was carried out entirely by officers
options.misconception: treats silence as absence, when the crews of such a fleet are precisely what a ceremonial account omits

options.text: The account is unreliable throughout, since a document that leaves out the workers is not describing a real voyage
options.misconception: dismisses a whole source over one omission, when a record's omissions are informative about its purpose

questions.explanation: An official account is a description of a purpose, and the way to read it is to ask which questions it was written to answer. Here the categories are the fleet's size, the rank of the officers, the gifts and the reception, and those are exactly the categories of a diplomatic mission presented to foreign courts: a visiting power wants to be seen as large, orderly and generous. The absence of the crews is not a gap a reader should try to fill; it is the most informative thing about the document, because a ceremonial account is written for posterity and posterity does not want the rowing detail. So the record supports a strong conclusion about the voyage's purpose and a weak one about the conditions the sailors were in, and a reader who knows which is which can use the same document well. The distractors each fail on the treatment of evidence. B is the most tempting, since goods are listed, and the correction is that a gift is also goods and the listing of ranks beside them is what identifies the occasion. C repeats the error the previous item was built to catch. D is the overcorrection, and it is worth resisting firmly, because a source with a clear purpose is not a source that is unusable; it is a source that has to be read for what it was doing.
questions.hint: Ask which questions the document was written to answer, and treat the omission as part of the answer rather than as a gap.

questions.topic: Order of a dynastic interregnum
questions.learningObjective: order the events of a collapse and the succession that followed it
questions.stem: Four stages of one collapse and the succession that followed it have been listed out of order by a class. Only one sequence is the order in which the events occurred. Which sequence is it?

options.text: 原有的王朝灭亡 / 有人称帝并改换国号 / 各地爆发起义 / 原来的王朝在南方重建
有人称帝并改换国号 / 原有的王朝灭亡 / 各地爆发起义 / 原来的王朝在南方重建
原有的王朝灭亡 / 各地爆发起义 / 有人称帝并改换国号 / 原来的王朝在南方重建
有人称帝并改换国号 / 各地爆发起义 / 原有的王朝在南方重建 / 原来的王朝灭亡

questions.explanation: The sequence is the first one, and the order is not a matter of memory but of cause. The old dynasty ends first, because the usurpation in the second stage is a consequence of that ending and cannot precede it. The new ruler then takes the throne and changes the dynastic name, which is the act that makes the interregnum a separate period rather than a disputed episode within the old one. The uprisings come third, and the reason they come third rather than first is what makes the period short: a regime that has taken the throne by succession and is governing as a usurper is broadly accepted for a time, and the opposition grows afterwards as the failure to produce order accumulates. The restoration comes last, and the word for it is the one the sequence hinges on, because the restored line is the old dynasty resumed in a different place, at a different capital, over a smaller territory, and with a different relation to the power to the north. A reader who knows that the restoration was a continuation with a smaller base will not be surprised by the difference between the two periods that share a name. The second option has the usurpation before the fall, which inverts cause and effect. The third has the uprising before the new dynasty is proclaimed, which is possible in a general sense and wrong in this one, since the risings are what ended the interregnum rather than what began it. The fourth is a chain in which nothing follows from anything.
questions.hint: Ask which of the four stages is the cause of the one after it, and what the restored dynasty shares with the fallen one.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: What a collapse leaves behind
questions.learningObjective: distinguish what a dynastic change carries over from what it discards
questions.stem: When a dynasty is replaced after a long collapse, the new rulers keep the law, the writing, the ritual and the administrative offices, and change the family in power. What is the most useful way to describe that?

options.text: A change of dynasty rather than a change of system, since the institutions outlast the house that took them over
A continuity with no change at all, since the only difference between the two is a question of which family is in power
options.misconception: reduces a change of dynasty to a family matter and so denies that anything in the country changed

options.text: A revolution, because the transfer of power from one house to another always required the people to rise
options.misconception: confuses a change of rulers with a change of society, which are different events with different evidence

options.text: A restoration, because an institution kept in use has by definition gone back to the state it came from
options.misconception: infers continuation from survival, when keeping an institution is the opposite of restoring the arrangement around it

questions.explanation: The distinction between a dynasty and a system is the single most useful tool a student of this subject can acquire, and the evidence for it is exactly what the case provides. The law continues, so a contract signed under the old house is still judged by the same rule; the offices continue, so the same men hold the same posts; the ritual continues, so the calendar and the ceremonies do not move. What changes is the family, and with it the distribution of the highest posts and the character of the court. To call that a change of dynasty is accurate and it is not a dismissal: a change of dynasty can be a very large event for the people who live through it, and the phrase describes the institution rather than the experience. The point to be careful about is the temptation to make the label carry a moral verdict in either direction, in which case the label stops describing anything. The distractors each make that slide. B treats continuity as though nothing changed, which flattens the one thing that did. C reaches for the strongest available word on the strength of a change of rulers. D is the subtler and the most instructive, because it treats a surviving institution as evidence that the whole arrangement came back, when in this case the dynasty that is restored is a different dynasty that happens to share a name with the fallen one and to occupy a smaller part of its territory.
questions.hint: Ask which institutions are still running after the change, and which of the two things the case says has actually been replaced.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: The logic of a move south
questions.learningObjective: explain the political logic behind a forced change of capital
questions.stem: After losing the northern part of its territory to an invading power, a court moved its capital south, beyond the invaders' reach, and governed what was left from there. Which reading of that decision is the best one?

options.text: The move preserved the state by exchanging a lost land for a defensible one, and the new capital sat at the centre of the economy that was left
The move was an admission that the state had ended, so the southern court was a government in name only
options.misconception: reads a reduction in territory as the end of a state, when a court that governs anything is still a state

options.text: The move was a diplomatic solution, since moving the court put the two parties in one place and made negotiation possible
options.misconception: reinterprets a retreat as an attempt at negotiation, when the decision followed the loss rather than preceding it

options.text: The move was administrative convenience, since the southern capital was simply the largest city available to the survivors
options.misconception: reduces a decision about the state's survival to a question of buildings

questions.explanation: A move of this kind is a calculation about survival, and there are two things in the calculation, which is why a good answer names both. The first is geography: the court moved beyond the reach of the power that had taken the north, choosing a region where the rivers, the harbours and the terrain made a large army difficult to bring. The second, and the more instructive, is that the new capital sat inside the economy that was left. The best farmland, the densest population, the busiest ports and the productive workshops were all in the south, and a government that has lost the north but holds the south is not a rump: it has the tax base, the manpower and the trade on which a later recovery depends, and a court that governs that from a capital inside it is governing its country's centre of gravity rather than its edge. That is the logic worth extracting, because it recurs whenever a state is pushed onto a smaller base. The distractors each collapse the decision. B treats a loss of territory as a loss of existence, which is a confusion between a state and its maximum extent. C turns a retreat into a diplomatic opening, and it has the causality backwards. D is the reduction a reader makes when a question sounds administrative, and it explains nothing, since a capital is chosen for reasons that are never merely the number of buildings available.
questions.hint: Ask what the new capital was the centre of, and what a court keeps when it has lost the northern half of its territory.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: What a capital reveals
questions.learningObjective: infer what a capital's position indicates about a state's priorities
questions.stem: A court sits at a capital with a very large population, busy workshops, a busy market and a river that carries ocean-going ships, and no defensible walls against attack from the north. What does that combination indicate?

options.text: That the state's priorities are commercial and administrative rather than military, so the capital is placed where revenue and trade are rather than where a campaign would be fought
That the state had no enemies, since a capital that is not fortified is a capital nobody has thought about attacking
options.misconception: reads a gap in the defences as an absence of threat, when the more usual explanation is a deliberate choice

options.text: That the court had recently lost a war and moved in haste, since a new capital is never built inside a large and busy city
options.misconception: assumes a new capital must be a small place, which the size of this one contradicts

options.text: That the capital was chosen for the view, since a river city with shipping is a more pleasant seat than an inland one
options.misconception: gives a preference as an explanation where a commercial calculation is available

questions.explanation: A capital's position is a statement of priorities, and a reader who learns to ask this question can infer a great deal from a map. A very large population, workshops, a market and an ocean-going river are the features of a place that produces and trades, and a court that sits there has chosen to be near the revenue and near the merchants rather than near a frontier or a military centre. The absence of defences against a northern approach then stops being a weakness and becomes information: the state is not expecting to be attacked from there, and the reason is that the capital's value is in what it collects and circulates, which is lost to an invader who takes it. That is a different arrangement from the one in which a court sits behind walls in a river valley, and the difference between them is a difference about where a state thinks its strength is. The distractors each convert a feature into a mistake in reasoning. B treats a missing wall as proof of an absent threat. C assumes a new capital must be small and imposes a chronology the size contradicts. D is the reduction that is easy to make and never explains anything, since a view is a preference and a capital is a calculation. The general habit worth taking from this item is to ask what the capital was for, and to notice that the answer is usually about where the state's money is made rather than about where its enemies are.
questions.hint: Ask what a capital placed in a large trading city is close to, and what the missing northern defences imply.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: Exchange under a conquest dynasty
questions.learningObjective: describe the character of cultural exchange under a conquest dynasty
questions.stem: A dynasty founded by an outside conquering people ruled China as part of a much larger empire stretching far into Central Asia. What is the most defensible statement about the cultural exchange of that period?

options.text: The empire's overland networks carried people, goods, techniques and beliefs in both directions, so the period is best described as increased contact rather than a one-way import
The period was one of sealed exchange, since a foreign dynasty in China kept the two traditions carefully apart
options.misconception: describes a state that was itself the product of the contact it is supposed to have prevented

options.text: The period produced a fusion in which the conquering people adopted everything from the conquered and gave nothing in return
options.misconception: turns a two-way exchange into a one-way borrowing, which the record of the period does not support in either direction

options.text: The period changed little, since a change of dynasty does not by itself alter the culture of a country
options.misconception: generalises from the earlier point about continuity, which applies to institutions and not to everything

questions.explanation: The governing fact about this period is that China was inside a continental empire, and that fact is the mechanism of the exchange. A single power stretching from China to Central Asia and Persia kept open the overland routes for merchants, missionaries, craftsmen and envoys, and a traveller could move a long way without changing allegiance. That is why the period shows foreign musical instruments, new styles in painting, new foods, new forms of dress and a Persian or Central Asian element in court culture, and it is also why the exchange ran the other way: Chinese goods, ceramics and technologies travelled west, and the dynasty itself was a product of the connections it later governed. A good answer will also say what the fusion was not, and there are two things to exclude. It was not sealed exchange, which is contradicted by the fact that the ruling house was itself foreign and had arrived along those routes. And it was not a one-way borrowing in which the conquerors took everything and gave nothing, because the interesting part of the period is that the traditions mixed and the mixture stayed recognisably Chinese in its essentials while being visibly unlike what came before. The distractors each close the exchange off. B closes it, C makes it one-directional, and D generalises the earlier distinction between a change of dynasty and a change of system, which was correct about institutions and is wrong about the whole of a culture.
questions.hint: Ask what the extent of the empire made possible, and in which directions the movement of goods and ideas ran.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: Testing a claim about a period of contact
questions.learningObjective: diagnose a claim about cultural exchange and state what would test it
questions.stem: Stage one: a claim says that during a period when China was part of a large continental empire, cultural influence flowed in only one direction, from outside to inside. Diagnose what is wrong with the shape of that claim. Stage two: say what kind of evidence would show movement in the other direction, and why the absence of such evidence would be weak.

answer.exemplar: Stage one. The claim fails before any fact is examined, because a claim about cultural influence has to be symmetrical to be checkable at all, and this one has removed one of the two directions in advance. It is not that the direction is wrong; it is that the claim has been shaped so that half the possible evidence would count against it and the other half would not. Consider what is available. A new instrument or a foreign technique appearing in Chinese practice is exactly the same kind of item as a Chinese technique appearing in Central Asian practice, and a claim built to count only the first has arranged itself to be unfalsifiable in one direction. There is a second structural problem, which is that the claim confuses a period with a border. China was inside the empire and the routes ran through it, so the period is not a relationship between two sealed societies with a single direction of movement; it is one large connected space in which things travel, and a claim about a connected space that asserts a single flow is a claim that needs a mechanism as well as a fact. Stage two. The evidence that would show movement outward is of the same kind as the evidence for movement inward and comes from the other end. Objects found outside China and dated to the period, which is why a find in a Central Asian city is as probative as one in a Chinese one. Foreign texts that describe Chinese goods in use. Chinese techniques or products recorded in Central Asian sources. And the ordinary documentary trace: a record of a Chinese craft, a coin, a design or a dish outside the Chinese border. What makes the absence of this evidence weak is the structure of the archive, and this is the part worth insisting on. Survival is uneven, and the record is much fuller on one side of the empire than the other, so a traveller looking for outward movement will find it harder to find than a traveller looking for inward movement, and the reason is the archive rather than the history. The correct conclusion is therefore not that the claim is false, nor that it is true, but that a one-directional claim about a connected period is the wrong shape, and the right procedure is to treat both directions as open until the records have been looked at on both sides.

questions.explanation: The exemplar is marked correct for locating the fault in the claim's shape rather than in a fact, and for the point that an uneven archive makes one direction harder to find. A response that says the claim is false because a particular item travelled outward has answered a different question from the one the diagnosis asked for.
questions.hint: Ask what would count as evidence against the claim, and ask why one direction of the search is easier than the other.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: The basis of the 1898 reform attempt
questions.learningObjective: state the intellectual sources of a late nineteenth-century reform movement
questions.stem: In 1898 a group of reformers at court tried to change the examination system, the schools and the administration within a few months. Where did the argument for that programme come from?

options.text: From a Chinese tradition of arguing that institutions should be examined and improved, joined to translations of Western political writing that had begun to circulate in the 1890s
From foreign envoys, who told the court that no state could remain strong while it examined its candidates on the classical texts
options.misconception: invents an external instruction, when the argument was made by reformers inside the tradition they were changing

options.text: From a military defeat, since a defeat produces a conviction that the whole system is at fault rather than only the weapons
options.misconception: attributes a conviction to a shock, when a defeat produced several different responses and this was only one

options.text: From the traders, who had seen abroad and came back convinced that the examination system was the obstacle to national wealth
options.misconception: narrows the movement to a group's experience, when its published arguments drew on two traditions at once

questions.explanation: The reform is best understood as a reform made inside a tradition rather than an import into one, and that is the point an answer has to get right. The Chinese side of the argument is a long-standing one: there was already a body of writing that treated institutions as things to be examined, that had earlier criticised the examination system for testing memorisation, and that supplied the vocabulary for arguing that a state should be reorganised. The Western side arrived through translations of political and social writing carried out in the 1890s, which gave reformers a second vocabulary and, more importantly, the example of states that had reorganised and prospered. The programme is what you would expect from the combination: the examination system, schools, universities, and a rebuilt administration. A reader should also note why this matters for judging the movement, because a reform framed as a return to a proper Chinese principle was very much harder for the established authorities to answer than a reform framed as foreign imitation, and the framing is therefore part of the politics rather than decoration. The distractors each invent a single external source. B puts the argument in foreign mouths. C mistakes a shock for a cause of conviction, since a defeat generated more than one response. D makes it a report by travellers, which is far too thin for a programme that had been argued in print for years.
questions.hint: Ask whether the argument was made inside the tradition or brought into it, and what the translations supplied.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: Why a short reform failed
questions.learningObjective: explain the structural reasons a reform programme of a few months could not succeed
questions.stem: Explain in your own words why a programme that changed the examination system, the schools and the administration at once had little chance of surviving a few months, and say what a reform with a realistic prospect would have had to give up.

answer.exemplar: The programme failed for a structural reason rather than a bad one, and the distinction matters because it tells a reader what to look for in other reforms. A change of this size creates opponents at every level at once. The examination system was the road into office, so changing it put at risk the investment of every family that had spent a generation preparing for it, and that is a very large body of people with an interest in the existing arrangement. The schools that the reform proposed would have taken resources and prestige away from the institutions that taught the classics. The administration it proposed to rebuild would have displaced incumbents, and a displaced official is not a neutral witness to a policy. Each of these groups has a reason to resist that survives the failure of any individual argument, and a programme that raises all three at once has organised all three into a single front. There is a second structural point, which is the length of time such change actually requires. Building a school system, training teachers and moving a civil service onto a new basis are works of decades, and a programme that announces all of them in a season is announcing something the state cannot deliver at any speed, so the expectation it creates is one that will be disappointed. The only resource that made the 1898 attempt possible was the position of a small group close to the throne, and that is also its weakness, because it means the programme had no support of its own outside the one place where it could be stopped. What a reform with a realistic prospect has to give up is therefore the attempt to do everything at once, and this is the same principle as the earlier point about an ordinary budget: a plan has to survive being wrong about one of its parts, and a programme that requires every part to succeed has no margin. The realistic version would begin where the opposition is weakest and where an early success could be demonstrated, and would build a constituency while the institution changed. That costs years and it looks, from inside, like doing too little.

questions.explanation: The exemplar is marked correct for explaining the failure through the interests the programme endangered rather than through the quality of the ideas, for treating the single-institution origin as a weakness, and for stating what must be given up as scope rather than as conviction. A response that says the reform was too radical has named a property and not a mechanism.
questions.hint: Ask who lost something from each of the three changes, and how long the underlying work actually takes.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: What the self-strengthening programme built
questions.learningObjective: describe the scope and the limit of the self-strengthening programme
questions.stem: From the 1860s, officials in several provinces built arsenals and a shipyard, laid a telegraph line, and opened schools for technical subjects, all financed from their own regional funds. What is the best summary of that programme?

options.text: A serious attempt to acquire modern military and technical means, which left the political structure of the state untouched and therefore left the weakness that mattered
A programme of political reform that happened to include factories, since rebuilding the state and building its weapons were one project
options.misconception: reverses the two halves of the programme, when the political structure is precisely what the programme did not touch

options.text: A policy of opening the country to foreign trade, since imported machinery and imported teachers were its principal content
options.misconception: confuses the tools the programme bought with the policy the programme belonged to

options.text: An unsuccessful effort, since a programme that did not prevent defeat in 1895 can have achieved nothing at all
options.misconception: judges the whole by one outcome, when the arsenals and the schools were real and the defeat was about something else

questions.explanation: The programme has to be judged on two axes at once, and holding both is the whole of the item. On the first it was real: new arsenals, a modern shipyard, a telegraph, and schools teaching mathematics, chemistry, engineering and languages produced officers, technicians and a naval force that did not exist a generation earlier, and the railways and steamships acquired in the same period changed what the state could do. On the second it stopped exactly where the decision was: the structure of government, the examination system and the political authority of the court were left as they were, and the funds came from regional officials rather than from a central plan, which is itself a continuation of the arrangement the state would later need to change. The limit is therefore not a failure of effort but a choice about where to stop, and the decisive evidence for the choice being wrong came in 1895, when a modern fleet lost to a modern fleet. A reader should be careful to say what that defeat demonstrated: it demonstrated that weapons do not substitute for the organisation, the revenue and the command that produce them, and a programme that buys the weapon has not addressed any of the three. The distractors each move the boundary. B absorbs the programme into political reform, which inverts it. C confuses the imported tools with the policy, and a policy of opening is a different project with a different set of supporters. D is the flat verdict, and it is the one to resist, because it discards a decade of genuine institutional building because of a single later event.
questions.hint: Ask what the programme changed and where it stopped, and which of those two facts the defeat of 1895 bears on.

questions.topic: A defeat read two ways
questions.learningObjective: weigh two readings of the same defeat against what each can support
questions.stem: A state with a recently built modern navy loses a war to a state with a newer one. One writer concludes the navy was useless and the whole programme a waste. Another concludes that the programme was necessary and merely incomplete. Which comparison of the two is fairest?

options.text: The first reading takes one outcome and generalises it to the whole programme, while the second separates the outcome from the programme and asks what the gap actually consisted of
The first reading is sound, because a programme that ends in defeat has been shown by its result not to have worked

options.misconception: mistakes necessity for sufficiency, which is exactly the gap the defeat exposed

The general lesson is worth more than the case, and it applies to any institution built over years: an outcome tests the part of the system that produced the outcome, and a reader who has to say which part that was has already done the important thinking. C is the second reading overstated, because being necessary and having been sufficient are different claims and only one of them is being made. D abandons a question that the record answers well, and it is worth noticing that this retreat is usually available and is sometimes a way of avoiding an answer.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: What a defeat set off
questions.learningObjective: identify the consequences a military defeat set in motion
questions.stem: In 1895 a war was lost and a treaty ceded territory and required a large indemnity. Which of the following is a direct consequence of that defeat?

options.text: Foreign powers competed for leases and influence in China, and the pressure for institutional reform at home intensified
The navy that had been built was dismantled, since a navy which lost cannot be of any use to a state
options.misconception: assumes a total loss of capacity where the defeat was military and the fleet continued in service

options.text: The examinations were abolished, since the defeat is usually blamed on a system that examined the wrong things
options.misconception: brings forward a later change and treats it as an immediate effect of the war

options.text: The western powers withdrew from the region, having concluded that the country was not worth investing in
options.misconception: predicts withdrawal when the defeat made the country more valuable as a place to invest

questions.explanation: A defeat is best read by asking what it made newly possible for other people, and here the answer is a scramble. A state that has lost territory and paid a large indemnity is a state that other powers now expect to be able to influence, and the years after 1895 saw foreign powers obtaining leases, spheres of influence, and commercial privileges under the pressure of a weakened government. The same weakening is what produced the argument at home that institutions, not weapons, were the problem, so a political reform movement that had been marginal became urgent. Both consequences flow from the same fact, which is what makes the two of them a single consequence rather than two facts. Three further cautions are worth adding because the period is often taught too simply. The war was not the whole of the nineteenth century and its effects are not confined to this one. The indemnity and the leases were matters of state finance and of foreign presence, and they interacted with a domestic fiscal crisis that preceded them. And the reform impulse produced several programmes rather than one, so a reader who treats the defeat as having a single consequence will be surprised by the range. The distractors each assert an outcome the record does not support. B is the claim that a military defeat retires an institution, which is wrong in this case. C assigns to a war a change that came later and by other hands. D has the incentive exactly backwards.

It is a term the states involved used at the time, so a document from 1890 would use it in exactly this sense
options.misconception: assumes a later label was the contemporary description, which is a question about dating and not about the pattern

options.text: It is a neutral periodisation, like the names for the dynasties, and so it makes no judgement about what happened
options.misconception: reads a name with a judgement in it as if it were merely a label

options.text: It describes a continuous state of subjugation, so no event within it can properly be called resistance
options.misconception: turns a period name into an account that rules out everything that happened inside it

questions.explanation: A period name is a piece of historiography and has to be handled like one. The label is retrospective: it was applied to a stretch of history afterwards, by writers for whom the pattern was already visible, and the fact that it is retrospective does not make it wrong. What it names is real and specific, and a reader can state it precisely. During that stretch, a series of wars and treaties imposed conditions on a previously sovereign state that were unequal by design: foreign troops stationed on Chinese soil, foreign officials exercising jurisdiction over their own nationals in Chinese cities, tariffs fixed by treaty rather than by the Chinese government, and cessions of territory. Those are checkable facts about institutions and not judgements about national feeling. Naming the period after that pattern is defensible and useful, and it is also the case that the label has a use and a hazard, which a reader should hold at once. The use is that it prevents a period being described as a series of unrelated events. The hazard is that a name which contains a verdict can do the work of an argument: once a period is called humiliating, resistance within it can be described as impossible or as irrelevant, and the resistance of the period, which is considerable, disappears from the account. The distractors each take the wrong side of that tension. B asserts a contemporary use that a later coinage excludes. C treats a value-laden name as value-free. D is the failure this item is really about, and a reader who falls into it has allowed a label to eliminate the events it covers.

questions.stem: The revolution of 1911 ended a monarchy that had ruled for centuries, and the movement that led it published a programme. Which statement about that programme is the most defensible?

It called for the restoration of the monarchy with new powers for the old court, since the aim was reform and not replacement
options.misconception: inverts the programme, when a republic was the published objective and the old court was made to abdicate

The three principles attached to the movement name what that republic was to be: nationalism, democracy, and the people's livelihood, and the third is the one a modern reader most needs explained, because it names a commitment about economic conditions rather than about institutions alone. The programme is evidence about the leadership's stated intentions, and those intentions did not all survive the transfer of power, which is the subject of the next item. And the principles were the most radical of the claims made at the time rather than the most widely shared: provincial assemblies, commercial groups and much of the gentry who had joined the movement were not asking for everything the programme named. B has the movement restoring what it ended. C imports the older pattern. D is the error that makes the question unaskable, and it is worth resisting, because a movement without a programme is a category the record simply does not contain.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: What a treaty establishes
questions.learningObjective: explain what a treaty changes beyond the terms it names
questions.stem: Explain in your own words what the 1842 treaty changed besides the territory it ceded and the ports it opened, and why the terms it fixed were the more durable part.

answer.exemplar: The cession and the opened ports are the clauses a reader remembers, and they are the less important ones, because both are arrangements between two states about particular places. What the treaty changed permanently was the position of the Chinese state inside its own country, and it did that with three mechanisms that had nothing to do with territory. First, an agreed tariff. Before it, the Chinese state set its own duties on foreign goods; after it, the rates were fixed by agreement and could not be raised at will, so the revenue side of the state became partly a foreign-negotiated quantity. That is a structural change, and it is the one that took longest to undo. Second, agreed rules of extraterritoriality, under which foreign nationals were subject to their own law rather than the law of the place they were in, so a Chinese court could not try a foreign subject and a Chinese official could not enforce a judgment against one. That created a category of person inside Chinese territory beyond the reach of Chinese law, and nothing about the treaties' other clauses can be understood without it. Third, the ports themselves became places where a foreign official had a standing presence, which meant that the sovereignty a Chinese official exercised stopped at the boundary of a foreign quarter, an arrangement a Chinese official found intolerable precisely because it was visible every day. The general point is the one worth taking away, and it is about the difference between a clause and a structure. A clause transfers something. A structure changes the capacity of a state, and it does so by removing a discretion that a government had previously exercised without question. That is why these terms outlasted the cessions: a piece of land can be recovered or lost again, while a state's ability to set its own tariff or to try its own subjects has to be deliberately rebuilt, and no subsequent event rebuilt it as part of any one negotiation. So a reader should ask, of any treaty in this period, what discretion the state kept afterwards, and that question reaches further into the century than any list of places.

questions.explanation: The exemplar is marked correct for separating the territorial clauses from the three that changed the state's capacity, for naming the tariff and the jurisdiction of foreign nationals as mechanisms rather than as grievances, and for the general principle that a structure outlasts a clause because a clause transfers something while a structure removes a discretion. A response that lists the concessions has reported the treaty without analysing it.
questions.hint: Ask what the Chinese state could still decide for itself after the treaty, and which of those decisions the terms removed.

Each agreement in the sequence was concluded at a moment when the Chinese state had just lost a war or was in the middle of one, and the terms of each reflect the balance at that moment. Reading them together therefore gives something a single document cannot: a measure that keeps moving, which is to say a record of decline that can be examined at several points rather than asserted once. The pattern was cumulative, because an agreement with one power became a precedent others used, and so the terms with the second were worse than the terms with the first. And the obligations were open-ended, since the most-favoured-nation formula meant that any concession granted to one power had to be extended to all, which meant a Chinese state could not grant a new privilege to anybody without granting it to everybody. C removes the sovereignty question by relocating the agreements, which is not available. D is a legal assertion offered without support, and it is the one to be most careful with, because claims resting on it have been made and the point deserves checking rather than repetition.

questions.stem: A new state adopts a constitution with a president, a cabinet responsible to parliament, and a parliament elected by a broad franchise. What must exist in the country for that design to work, and what happens if it does not?

A written constitution alone, since the document supplies the mechanism and the politics will follow the document
options.misconception: treats an institutional design as self-executing, which is the assumption behind most failed parliamentary settlements

options.text: A tradition of judicial independence, since a president with the courts behind him will be checked and the cabinet will answer to the judges

questions.explanation: A parliamentary design is a machine for turning votes into governments, and a machine needs a part that supplies the movement. Parties are that part, and it is worth being precise about what they do, because the mechanism is not simply that they organise voters. A party is a group that agrees in advance what it will do if it wins a majority, so that when it has one, the people in it know they must act together to form a government; and it is a group that has organised enough seats to be the plausible loser, so that a government which loses an election has a reason to leave.
