That is the general point, and it recurs whenever a constitutional arrangement is imported faster than the organisation around it can develop. The distractors each substitute a different source of stability. B assumes a document is self-executing, which is the assumption behind a great many constitutional failures. C assigns the cabinet-making function to the courts, which do not have it. D confuses the size of an electorate with the structure of a legislature, and a reader who keeps those separate will notice immediately that a very broad franchise and a very weak parliament can exist together.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: Choosing a priority and paying for it
questions.learningObjective: explain what concentrating investment on one sector means for the others
questions.stem: Explain in your own words why a decision to put most investment into heavy industry raised a political question about who was being asked to wait, and why the decision was defended in terms of a sequence.

answer.exemplar: Concentrating investment is a distributional decision before it is an economic one, and the distributional question is sharp enough to be stated in one sentence: the resources that went into a steel plant went into the steel plant, and somebody did not get them. A plan that fixes the share of national investment available to heavy industry fixes it by implication for everything else, so the choice between sectors is a choice about who bears the present cost of a future benefit. The two parties to that bargain were easy to name. Capital goods industries produce steel, machinery and chemicals, and they sell to other industries and to the state; consumer goods, agriculture and housing produce what people eat and live in, and they sell to households. Putting the investment into the first means the second had less to work with, and a household that had been promised a flat, a school or a better price for its grain was being asked to wait. That is why the decision is a political question and not only an economic one, and why a plan of this kind is never only a technical document. The defence was made in terms of a sequence, and the sequence is the whole argument. The claim was that heavy industry is upstream: without steel, machinery and power, every other industry is limited by what it can buy, so a country that has not built the upstream sectors cannot expand the downstream ones at any rate, however much it invests. On that account the first stage was not a permanent preference for one sector but a foundation, and the intended sequence was that the consumer industries would follow as the upstream capacity became available. This is a serious argument and it is the one a good answer should present at its strongest, because it does explain why some countries took this route and reached industrial capacity. It is also, and the second thing a good answer must say, an argument that the later record did not settle in the plan's favour on the timetable the plan expected. A consumer who waits for the sequence to deliver is making a bet on the timetable, and the people with the least tolerance for waiting are the ones with the least cushion. So the useful conclusion is not that the priority was right or wrong. It is that a priority is a promise about a future ordering, and any reader of a plan should ask two things: what the ordering assumes about how long each stage takes, and who bears the cost if the second stage is late. A plan that answers neither of those has not been read.

A response that says the priority was chosen for strategic reasons has not answered the question asked, which was about who waited.

The stated goal is developmental: to develop production, to make the country poorer no longer, and to raise the standard of living. The instruments are what a reader should study, because they are where the interesting disagreements were and they are not the same across decades. Giving households responsibility for their own plots changed what a household was paid for and raised agricultural output within a few years. Giving enterprises a margin of retained profit made their managers answer to a price rather than only to a plan. Opening special zones, with lower duties on imported equipment and tax concessions, invited foreign firms into a small number of places where the cost of being wrong was lowest. And admitting outside investment supplied capital and, just as importantly, a model of how a firm is run. The sequencing is the other thing worth stating, because the order of the instruments is itself an argument: farming first, then industry, then the parts of the economy that require a developed financial system, and the later steps were not available until the earlier ones had worked. Two cautions keep this from being read as a description of outcomes. The goals are what was stated, which is evidence about the leadership's intentions and not about what happened. And the instruments were unevenly applied and unevenly withdrawn, so a policy described by its instruments needs the record of the exceptions. The distractors each substitute a different policy: B describes a single-step abolition, C inverts the name, and D borrows a later slogan.

questions.topic: The logic of a special zone
questions.learningObjective: explain why economic experiments were first run in a few places
questions.stem: From 1980, four small coastal areas were given the power to waive duties on imported equipment, to offer tax concessions, and to set their own rules in some administrative matters. What is the logic of doing this in four places rather than everywhere?

options.text: A new policy has to be demonstrated where the cost of getting it wrong is contained, so a small number of places can be treated as tests and the results argued from
A new policy has to be applied where foreign firms wanted to go, so the zones were placed on the coast for geographical reasons alone
options.misconception: gives a real factor and stops, when the coastal placement and the experimental function are two different explanations

options.text: A new policy has to be visible to prove it is real, so a showcase was arranged where foreign journalists and merchants could see it working
options.misconception: reduces the zones to publicity, and a visible experiment still has to be allowed to fail

options.text: A new policy has to be reversible, and only a small area can be allowed to abandon it, so the zones were made revocable from the start
options.misconception: reverses the logic, since a zone that can be revoked at will has no security for the firms that invested in it

questions.explanation: The word zone contains the argument, and unpacking it explains the whole arrangement. A zone is a bounded piece of country inside which different rules apply, and it is used when a policy is too new to be applied everywhere at once, because the alternative is a national experiment in which a failure cannot be contained. Inside a zone the consequences of a mistake fall on that zone: the firms that took the concessions, the local administration, and the officials who approved them. That is what makes the experiment informative, since the information a reader wants is what happens when the rules are relaxed, and a zone supplies that at a cost the rest of the country does not pay. The three concessions are also worth reading as a package rather than a list. Duties waived on imported equipment is an input-side measure, because the point is to let a factory buy the machine it needs cheaply. Tax concessions are an output-side measure, and they are the part that most directly tests whether a lower cost produces more investment. Administrative latitude is a different kind of concession altogether, because it lets a local government act without waiting for a decision from a capital several hundred miles away, and it is the concession that a later reform generalised more widely. The distractors each offer a real factor as if it were the whole. The coastal location is true and is partly commercial, but it does not explain why the rules differ inside the boundary. C reduces the zones to publicity, and a zone that had to look good would not be a useful test. D gets the logic backwards, since a revocable concession is not an inducement to invest.
questions.hint: Ask what would have happened to the country as a whole if the new rules had been applied everywhere at once.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: What an experimental zone can and cannot show
questions.learningObjective: weigh the inference available from a successful experiment in a bounded place
questions.stem: A special zone on a coast with few natural resources, thin local infrastructure and a very small population attracts more foreign investment than any other comparable area. Which inference from that fact is the strongest available?

options.text: The concessions were a substantial part of what attracted the investment, since the zone's own endowments do not account for the result
The concessions alone explain the result, since a place with no resources cannot attract investment for any other reason
options.misconception: makes the package a single cause, when a port, a location near a major market and a trained workforce are all candidates

options.text: The result shows that the same concessions would produce the same figure in any inland province, since the incentives are what mattered
options.misconception: generalises from one place to all places, which is precisely the step the zone was built to make safe

options.text: The result shows that the zone's advantages were irrelevant, since the same result appeared in a place with none
options.misconception: reads a result as a refutation of the factors, when the whole inference is that one of them mattered

questions.explanation: This is a question about what a natural experiment can support, and the answer depends on the fact that the zone's own endowments do not explain its result. A place with no minerals, poor transport, a small population and a shallow local economy should not have attracted heavy foreign investment, and the fact that it did means something about the environment was doing the work. Since the concessions are the thing that differed from the rest of the country, the natural inference is that they mattered a great deal, and that inference is stronger than one drawn from a place whose attractions would have brought investment in any case. What the case does not establish is the converse. It does not show that the concessions were the only cause, because a deep-water port, a position facing a large market, an administration willing to move quickly and a workforce available at low cost are all candidates, and any of them could have been part of the explanation. And it certainly does not show that the same concessions in an inland province would produce the same figure, which is the generalisation that is precisely what the zone was created to avoid, since the point of bounding the experiment was that the other conditions would not be the same. The practical lesson is to state the inference at the strength the design can bear: something about the concessions, in this place, under these other conditions. The distractors each push past that limit. B reduces a package to a single cause, C generalises to all places, and D is the odd one out, since it takes a result as a refutation of the factors that make the result possible.
questions.hint: Ask what the zone did not have, and what that rules out, and what it says nothing about.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: A currency reform and its disruption
questions.learningObjective: diagnose the disruption a currency reform caused and explain the mechanism
questions.stem: Stage one: in the mid-1990s the government replaced a dual exchange rate with a single rate set close to the market rate, and the state had to buy a large quantity of foreign currency at the new rate. Diagnose where the difficulty actually came from. Stage two: explain why a state that fixes a currency rate has to hold reserves, and what changes when it stops fixing.

answer.exemplar: Stage one. The difficulty did not come from the reform being drastic, and it is worth saying so because the usual account exaggerates on that point. The reform removed a rate at which the state had been buying and selling currency for official business, and replaced the two rates with one. What made it expensive was not the abolition of the second rate but the gap between the old official rate and the market rate, and the direction of that gap. The official rate had been kept lower than the market rate, which meant that buying foreign currency through the official channel was cheap for anyone who could use it, and a real business with a legitimate need for dollars was being undercharged. Unifying at the market rate therefore raised the price at which the state itself had to obtain foreign currency, and the state's own payments for imported equipment and for its external debts were now made at the higher figure. The burden of closing a gap that large fell entirely on the state, which had to bring its reserves to bear, and the difference between the two rates across the whole volume of official business is the size of the bill. That is a diagnosis in terms of a price gap and a balance sheet, and it is a much better one than the version in which a government simply raised a price and hurt exporters, because the hurt to exporters is a consequence and the gap is the cause. Stage two. A state that fixes its currency to something other than the market rate has taken on an obligation it cannot meet on its own. The obligation is supply: if the rate is set such that the currency is cheap to buy and expensive to sell, then more of it will be demanded than the state wants to supply, and more will be offered than it wants to buy, and the state has to make the difference. That is what reserves are for. A government holding a large stock of foreign currency is holding the ability to intervene in the market, to buy its own currency when the pressure is downward and sell it when the pressure is upward, and the size of the stock tells you how much pressure it can absorb before the rate has to move. The reform is best understood as the moment the state stopped carrying that obligation at an unsustainable price, and the cost of stopping it was paid once, in reserves, in exchange for not having to pay it again in a stock of currency that had to be defended. This is the general lesson about fixed rates in any economy, and it is worth a reader carrying it out of the history: a fixed price is a standing obligation, and an obligation that is priced too far from the market is a bill that keeps arriving until somebody pays it in a lump.

questions.explanation: The exemplar is marked correct for locating the cause in the gap between the official and the market rate rather than in the severity of the change, for distinguishing the consequence to exporters from the mechanism, and for explaining reserves as the means of meeting a supply obligation. A response that says the reform raised the value of the currency has given a symptom and not a mechanism.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two rates made foreign currency cheap, and what a state that fixes a rate has promised to do about the difference.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: Dependency ratios over a transition
questions.learningObjective: explain why a falling birth rate first relieved a burden and later raised one
questions.stem: For several decades a country had a very low dependency ratio: few children and a large working-age population. Later the ratio rose sharply as those large cohorts grew old. What explains the reversal?

options.text: The population first grew large while the birth rate was already low, so the children were few and the workers many, and later the same cohorts reached retirement and the workers became few
The birth rate fell twice, once in the 1960s and again after 1980, and each fall added dependants rather than removing them
options.misconception: treats a fall in the birth rate as adding dependants, when fewer children is a smaller dependent group

options.text: Life expectancy stopped rising, so the population aged because people were living no longer rather than because cohorts grew old
options.misconception: reverses the mechanism, since ageing comes from cohorts surviving and from fewer children following them

options.text: The working-age population moved abroad, so the ratio rose by migration alone with no change in the birth rate at all
options.misconception: finds a cause in a movement that did not occur at the scale the ratio requires

questions.explanation: A dependency ratio counts people who are not of working age against people who are, so what moves it is a change in the size of either group, and the two groups are not independent of each other. The sequence to hold in the mind is a demographic echo. A birth rate that falls leaves a small number of children; a small number of children is a small dependent group, and the adults of that generation are at work, so the ratio is low. Because births stayed low, the next generation is small as well, and the large working-age cohorts are supported by a small number of dependants. Then the same large cohorts reach old age, and they become dependants themselves while the cohorts behind them, having been born in small numbers, are too small to replace them. The ratio rises for a reason that is the mirror image of the reason it fell. That is the item worth taking away, and it corrects a habit of reading the low-ratio decades as a permanent improvement rather than as a stage. Three additions keep it usable. The policy that limited births is part of the explanation and is not the whole of it, since the low mortality that made large cohorts possible was already there. A low ratio is genuinely a window in which investment per child is high, which is why the period is studied. And the reversal arrives with a lag, which is why the danger of a low ratio is invisible at exactly the time it is being enjoyed.
questions.hint: Ask what a cohort of few children does to the ratio when it is young, and what it does when it is old.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: What a demographic shift obliges
questions.learningObjective: explain the pressure a low dependency ratio creates later
questions.stem: Explain in your own words why a period with a very low dependency ratio is often described as a window that has to be saved, and say what a government cannot do once the window has closed.

answer.exemplar: The description is a claim about a sequence and not about a favour, and the sequence is the whole of the point. When the number of dependants is small and the number of earners is large, the cost of bringing up a child is spread across many workers rather than few, and a family can treat a child as an investment rather than as a burden, because the arithmetic of the household says it will be repaid. A government in the same position can do the expensive, slow things: build schools, extend health coverage, put money where each additional teacher serves many more children than it would in a young population. Every one of these is cheaper while the ratio is low, and the mechanism is not a discount but a denominator. The second half of the description is that this is a window, and a window closes. It closes because the large cohorts age. The people who were the denominator are now the numerator, and the small cohorts behind them are too small to become a new denominator, so a government that has deferred a pension obligation to the low-ratio decades has simply accumulated a bill. The question of what cannot be done afterwards follows from the arithmetic of the body and not from a policy choice. A pension promised at a rate that assumed a large working population cannot be reduced to a lower rate later, because the people affected by the reduction are the same people who were promised the higher one. A school system sized to a young population cannot be made to serve an old one cheaply, because the demand has moved to a different service. And a decision to have fewer children cannot be revisited, since the people who were not born are exactly the people who would have to enter the workforce. So the honest statement is that a low ratio does not make anything free; it makes certain things cheaper to arrange once, and the arrangements that are cheap once are the ones that are worth making first. A reader who takes that away will understand why the period was argued about so fiercely and why the argument was largely about what to do before the window shut.

questions.explanation: The exemplar is marked correct for identifying the ratio's denominator as the mechanism that makes the period cheap, for the asymmetry between deferring an obligation and being able to withdraw one, and for the claim that a birth decision cannot be revisited. A response that says the window is an opportunity has described the benefit and not the reason it is called a window.
questions.hint: Ask what the ratio's denominator is doing while the ratio is low, and which of the resulting obligations can be withdrawn later.

questions.topic: A poet and a period
questions.learningObjective: place a named author and one work in the period that produced it
questions.stem: A Tang poet lived from 712 to about 770, was displaced from his home by a rebellion that began in 755, and was separated from his family for long periods. Which statement about him is a matter of historical fact?

options.text: He is Du Fu, and the disruption of the rebellion of the later 750s is the condition of the work for which he is remembered
He is Li Bai, whose poems belong to the same period but describe a world of travel and drinking rather than of displacement
options.misconception: confuses two poets of the same period, whose circumstances and subjects are well documented and different

options.text: He is a poet whose reputation was made in the Song century, when editors collected and ranked the poets of his own
options.misconception: assigns the reputation to a later century, which is when much of the ranking and collecting was done

options.text: He is a poet who was dismissed from office for writing about the war, since criticism of a rebellion was treated as a political offence
options.misconception: supplies a specific penalty that the record does not attach to him

questions.explanation: This is a question about placing a person, and the useful thing about it is that the answer is checkable rather than a matter of taste. Du Fu is dated 712 to about 770, which fixes him in the middle of the eighth century; the rebellion that began in 755 and ran to 763 is the event that displaced him, separated him from his family, and made the condition of his best-known work a ruined country and a wandering family. Those three facts together are enough to identify him, and a reader who knows them will not confuse him with the other great poet of the same period, who was of similar age and wrote about something else altogether. The pairing is worth drawing out rather than merely answering, because the two poets' subjects reflect their circumstances: one travelled widely and wrote about friendship, wine and the sights of a man with means, and the other was displaced and wrote about the state of the country. A reader who holds both is far better placed to read a line than a reader who holds one, because the subject of the poem starts to predict the tone. The distractors each fail on a fact. B swaps in the contemporary whose circumstances were the opposite. C moves the reputation forward a century, which is a real fact about literary history and not about this man's life. D attaches a specific penalty that is not part of the record and that a reader should be careful about, since invented details are the usual way a question of this kind goes wrong in study material.
questions.hint: Use the dates and the displacement together, and check whether the rebellion falls inside the poet's life.

questions.topic: Reading a poem as a historical record
questions.learningObjective: judge what a poem can and cannot establish as a historical fact
questions.stem: A student cites a poem that describes ruined walls, displaced families and conscription, and concludes that the period was one in which the population had fallen. Which evaluation is the fairest?

options.text: The poem is strong evidence that the writer saw a ruined country, and weak evidence about the size of the population, because a poem reports the experience of its author
The conclusion follows, since a poet who describes a ruined country is describing a country whose people had gone
options.misconception: infers a demographic fact from an image, which is the reasoning the item is built to catch

options.text: The poem is not evidence of anything, since poetry is a form of expression rather than a record
options.misconception: dismisses a whole class of source, when a poem is testimony about what its author saw

options.text: The poem is reliable evidence about the whole period, because a poet writing at the time had no reason to exaggerate
options.misconception: assumes a witness has no motive to select or shape, which is the assumption a reader must test

questions.explanation: The question is about the scope of a source, and the answer depends on taking a poem as a testimony and not as a measurement. A poem written by a displaced man about a country in which conscription and ruin had emptied whole districts is very good evidence that such things happened and that a writer experienced them, and it is the kind of source that no administrative return can improve on for the quality of the observation. What it cannot do is count. A population figure requires a census, a tax register, an estimate with a method, or the agreement of several such sources, and a poem supplies none of these: it reports what one person saw and what that person found moving. The general principle is worth stating as a habit, because it applies to every kind of source including official ones. Ask what a document is a record of, and then ask what question it can answer. An official return is excellent for what the state assessed and poor for what was actually collected, which is the same asymmetry one finds in a poem. The distractors each fail differently and each failure is instructive. B infers a measurement from an image, which is the commonest error in reading literature as evidence. C rejects a category of source outright, which is the overcorrection that leaves a reader with nothing. D grants a witness the absence of motive, and a reader who accepts that will apply it to every source and be wrong regularly.
questions.hint: Ask what kind of thing the source is a record of, and what a population figure would have to come from.

questions.topic: A modern author and the debates of the time
questions.learningObjective: place a modern work in the public arguments of its period
questions.stem: A short story published in 1921 gave its name to a character who rationalises every defeat and congratulates himself on his own honesty. Which context makes that choice of subject intelligible?

options.text: It was published when questions about the national character were being argued out in public, and the story takes a supposed self-image of the Chinese people as its object
It was published when the country was at war, and the character is an allegory of the invading army
options.misconception: supplies a wartime allegory, and the story is a satire of a self-image rather than an allegory of a foreign army

options.text: It was published as part of a campaign to promote a new literary style, and the subject was chosen only because the style required an ordinary speaker
options.misconception: reduces a literary choice to a stylistic campaign, which explains the language and not the subject

options.text: It was published in a journal whose editor required a character, so the subject follows the form of the publication
options.misconception: invents a condition of publication that the record does not support

questions.explanation: A literary choice is a response to something, and identifying the something is what turns a work into evidence about a period. The story in question is Lu Xun's, published in 1921 and named for a character whose name is a transliteration of a word meaning fool, a designation he takes as a compliment and who then supplies himself with a long series of explanations for why every defeat was somebody else's fault. The debate that makes that legible is the one about national character, which was being argued publicly in the years after the movement of 1919: was the country's difficulty a matter of a people who had been made servile, or of a system, or of an external order that had been imposed, and what could a writer do about it. A satire aimed at the first explanation is a literary act with a position, and it is why the story reads as an argument rather than as a character sketch. The point a reader should draw is the general one: a satirical target tells you what the author thought was worth attacking, and that is a fact about the public arguments of the period, not just about the story. Two cautions are worth adding. A satire is an argument and is best read as one, so it is evidence for the position of its author and not for the prevalence of the view it attacks. And the questions the debate raised are still open, which is why a reader who meets the story now finds the argument familiar rather than dated. The distractors each supply a context that is real in the period but not the one that explains this choice: a war, a stylistic campaign, and a condition of publication, none of which is the answer.
questions.hint: Ask what the story is an argument with rather than a description of, and what question its subject belonged to.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: Conceding the usual account in order to correct it
questions.learningObjective: apply a concessive structure to strengthen a literary judgement rather than weaken it
questions.stem: Stage one: a sentence says 与其说他写得不好, 不如说他不肯让读者轻松. Say what the structure does with the judgement and why the substitution strengthens it. Stage two: rewrite the flat sentence 这本书写得很差 in the same structure, and state what the rewrite commits the writer to.

answer.exemplar: Stage one. The structure takes a judgement that a reader already holds, concedes it, and then replaces it with a different one. The two halves are joined by a pair that means rather than and not the best said, so the first half cannot be the writer's own view: it is a description of what somebody else would say, placed where the reader can agree with it, and the second half is what the writer is proposing instead. That is why the construction strengthens a judgement rather than weakening it, and this is the point most readers get wrong. A writer who simply asserts that a book is bad is competing with every other assertion of badness, and the reader has no reason to prefer one. A writer who grants the ordinary objection and then reframes the book as deliberately difficult is making a different kind of claim, one the reader has to consider rather than repeat. What the second half names is an intention on the author's part, and intention is a different object from quality, so the argument moves from a comparison to an account of what the book is doing. Notice also that the concessive first half does work of a particular kind: it removes the objection the reader was about to make, and a reader whose objection has been removed cannot use it. Stage two. Applied to the flat sentence, the structure would concede that the book is poorly written and then propose that it is not trying to be easy, and the concession is the whole of the craft. What the rewrite commits the writer to is considerable, and a reader should be able to say what. The writer is committed to a claim about intention, which is a claim about the author's mind, and the author cannot be asked to confirm it, so the writer is standing behind an interpretation. The writer is also committed to the claim being defensible, since a book that is merely confusing is not being praised by this sentence; a writer who uses the structure to excuse a failure has said something different, and the difference is exactly whether the difficulty can be shown to be doing work. And the writer is committed to the concession being real, because a concession that is not a real version of the objection is a rhetorical gesture, and a reader who notices that will discount the rest. The general lesson is that a strong literary judgement usually begins by agreeing with something, and a flat assertion is what is left when the writer has not done the work of finding the agreement.

questions.explanation: The exemplar is marked correct for explaining the concessive first half as a removal of the reader's own objection, for moving the argument from quality to intention, and for naming what the rewrite commits the writer to rather than only producing one. A response that paraphrases the sentence has translated it and not analysed the structure.
questions.hint: Ask whose view the first half states, and what kind of claim the second half makes about the author rather than the book.

options.text: When the song was written, and for what occasion, since that fixes whether the present meaning was there at the start
On which occasions it was sung in the later period, since a song used at ceremonies is being asked to do political work
The gap between what the words describe and what the use now assigns them
Whether the association with the earlier place and period was ever recorded, or was made afterwards
How many times the song has been performed, since the number of performances measures the size of its audience
options.misconception: confuses a count of occasions with a measure of how many people were there

The occasions on which it was sung later are the second, because a song sung at a ceremony is being used, and a use is evidence of what the occasion required. The gap between words and use is the third, and it is the interesting one: the association with a place and a period is a claim about origin, and a claim about origin can be true, half true, or made later, and the difference matters for what the song is now doing. The fourth observation is the test of that claim, and it is the one a learner most often omits: was the connection ever recorded, or has it been made after the fact by people arranging the song's history. The fifth is the trap, and it is a natural one, because counting performances does feel like measuring. It does not. A performance is an occasion, and a song performed once in front of a million people and a song performed ten thousand times in front of three are indistinguishable by the count, so the number of performances measures the number of occasions and not the reach.

What is the most defensible statement about the discovery?

options.text: It shows that a remedy recorded in writing for sixteen centuries was a lead rather than a recipe, and that isolating and testing the compound was what made it a treatment
It shows that a recorded remedy was ineffective, since a plant cannot be used as a treatment
options.misconception: converts a lead into a verdict on the old record, which is the opposite of what the discovery demonstrates

options.text: It shows that modern research had rediscovered the whole of traditional pharmacology, since the compound was the plant's entire effect
options.misconception: turns the isolation of one compound into a validation of every recorded remedy

options.text: It shows that the scientific method cannot use traditional sources, since a lead that came from an old book was not a discovery at all
options.misconception: excludes a source from the method, which the result itself contradicts

It said nothing about which constituent did the work, in what quantity, or against which stage of the parasite, and those were the questions that had to be answered before the plant could be made into a reliable treatment. Tu Youyou's group isolated the compound, verified it against the disease, and the compound went on to become the basis of combination therapy for malaria, which is the part with a measurable effect on a population. questions.topic: A physician and public health practice
questions.learningObjective: describe what a physician's plague response established as practice
questions.stem: Around 1910 an outbreak of pneumonic plague spread through north-east China, and the response included the quarantine of contacts, disinfection of rooms and buildings, and the wearing of protective masks by medical staff. What is the most defensible statement about that response?

options.text: It combined measures aimed at the person, the place and the transmission, and it is remembered because it contained an outbreak that earlier responses to similar disease had not contained
It was the first attempt to treat the disease with a drug, since the measures named are the earliest record of a specific therapy
options.misconception: reads control measures as a treatment, which is the distinction the whole account turns on

options.text: It was rejected by the local authorities, who objected to quarantine on religious grounds, and it succeeded only after national troops intervened
options.misconception: supplies a specific obstruction and a specific rescue that the well-known account does not include

options.text: It established the germ theory of disease in China, since a doctor who identified a transmission route had demonstrated it
options.misconception: infers a theoretical revolution from a practical success, which is a much larger claim

questions.explanation: The response is significant for a reason that a reader can state, and it is worth being exact about the three kinds of measure, because the grouping is what generalises. Quarantine of contacts is a measure aimed at the person: it separates the sick from the well who have been exposed, and it works only if the identification of contacts is fast. Disinfection of rooms and buildings is a measure aimed at the place, and it matters here because pneumonic plague passes between people who are close to one another in an enclosed space, so a single infected building can seed a whole quarter. Protective masks are a measure aimed at the transmission itself, and the interesting historical detail is that the suggestion of a mask came from a Chinese doctor in that community, and Wu Lien-teh adopted it, refined it and enforced its use. He had no bacteriological confirmation at the time, so he acted on a clinical observation that a simple barrier cut the deaths among medical staff, and that is the interesting part: a measure adopted because it worked rather than because the theory had been established. The outbreak was contained, and Wu later built a public health service in Malaya, which is the second part of why the case is remembered. The distractors each replace the account with a different one. B turns control into cure. C adds an obstruction and a rescue that the standard account does not have, and a reader should be careful about adding detail. D is the overclaim, and it is the one to resist, since a practice can be right before the theory that explains it.
questions.hint: Ask which person, which place and which route the three measures act on, and what happened to the outbreak.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: Reading a low film output as evidence
questions.learningObjective: infer what a collapsed production figure indicates about a period
questions.stem: A study of Chinese cinema between 1966 and 1976 finds that only a handful of feature films were made, against dozens in the years before. Which inference from that figure is the best supported?

options.text: The industry was not producing, and the reason lies in the conditions of the decade rather than in a change of public taste
Public taste had turned against feature films, since a few films in ten years cannot be what an audience wanted
options.misconception: explains a production collapse by demand, when the studios were not making anything to be demanded

options.text: The films of that decade were all lost, so the low figure is a preservation problem rather than a production one
options.misconception: explains a production figure by a survival problem, and a reader should keep the two apart

options.text: The decade's output is a fair measure of what the country's cinema was, since a small output cannot represent a large industry
options.misconception: judges a record of a period by the completeness of the record, which is the assumption this item is built to break

questions.explanation: A production figure is a record about production, and reading it correctly means looking for what made the production impossible rather than for what the audience wanted. A fall from dozens of features a year to a handful across a whole decade is not a change in preference; a preference is a demand, and a demand cannot be satisfied by a film that was not made. So the collapse is a fact about the conditions of the decade: studios closed or were redirected, personnel were dispersed, and the political campaigns of the period made the production and circulation of films a hazardous business, so a small number were made under constraints and were then treated as models. The figure is therefore the most legible single indicator that an ordinary film history is not available for those years, and it is also the reason a scholar of that decade draws on other material. Three cautions keep this honest. The handful that were made are not unrepresentative of everything that was being made, because they were made under the same conditions, so they can be read for what the conditions allowed. A low figure is not the same as a lost archive, which is a different problem with a different cause, and the distinction matters because the first cannot be repaired by finding prints. And the inference points at conditions without establishing a particular cause, so an answer should say the collapse is explained by the conditions of the decade and should not attribute it to a single decree it has not seen. The distractors each replace the figure with a different kind of fact: B with demand, C with preservation, and D with a judgement about representativeness that the figure itself refutes.
questions.hint: Ask whether the films people did not want to see or the films nobody was allowed to make would produce this figure.

questions.topic: A costume drama and its audience
questions.learningObjective: infer what a mass audience for a period drama indicates about reception
questions.stem: A costume drama first broadcast in 1998 became a national conversation among people who did not normally watch the series, and studios began to produce more of the same. Which reading of that is the most defensible?

options.text: A genre that had been a specialist taste reached a mass audience, which told the producers that it could be sold widely, so the production of such series increased
Television audiences had become generally larger, since a single drama's popularity measures the size of the viewing public
options.misconception: reads one programme's audience as a measure of the whole audience, which is a different claim

options.text: The audience preferred period settings because they were cheaper to make, since cost explains both the popularity and the increase
options.misconception: supplies a production cost explanation for a viewing figure, and cost does not predict who watches

options.text: The series was made for the mass market from the start, so the later production of similar shows shows that the original plan had been correct
options.misconception: assumes a plan rather than a response, since the producers changed what they made after the result

questions.explanation: This is a question about how reception gets converted into production, and the chain in the keyed answer is the whole of it. A genre that had been watched by a limited audience did something that few things do, which is attract people who were not its intended audience, and the people who noticed most were the producers. Their conclusion was commercial rather than artistic: if viewers who did not normally watch this kind of series were watching it, the audience was larger than had been assumed, and the correct response to a market that turns out to be bigger than expected is to supply more of it. That is why the production of costume dramas increased through the following years, and the increase is therefore evidence about the earlier audience. The reasoning generalises beyond television and is worth stating as a rule for reading cultural history: a genre's history is best traced through the moments when its audience changes, since those are the moments when somebody's decision changes what gets made. Three cautions are worth carrying. A large audience does not mean the work was good, and the two judgements are independent. A rise in production does not establish that the later work was of the same quality, since producers responding to a demand rarely match the first success. And a national conversation is a fact about discussion, which is a different measure from viewing, and a reader should not use one for the other. The distractors each commit one of those errors: B generalises from one programme, C explains demand by cost, and D mistakes a response for a plan.
questions.hint: Ask who changed their mind, and what a change in what studios make afterwards tells you about the earlier audience.

questions.topic: A festival fixed by the calendar
questions.learningObjective: explain why a festival's date is fixed by a solar term rather than by a lunar month
questions.stem: One festival falls in early April every year and its main custom is sweeping the tombs and tending the ancestors. What fixes its date?

options.text: It is named after one of the twenty-four divisions of the solar year, so its date is set by the sun's position rather than by a lunar month
It is fixed by the second new moon of spring, so its date shifts within the lunar calendar from year to year
options.misconception: gives a lunar cause for a festival whose defining feature is that it does not shift

options.text: It was fixed by decree in a particular year, so the date is an administrative decision that a later government could change
options.misconception: supplies a date a later government could change, when the date is determined by the calendar

options.text: It marks the first warm day, so the custom is one that farmers chose when the ground became workable
options.misconception: supplies an agricultural explanation for a custom that is about the dead

questions.explanation: Qingming is the case that shows a reader how a festival's calendar basis can be identified from its behaviour, and the behaviour here is unusual. Most of the best-known festivals are set by the lunar calendar, which is why the date of the new year festival and the fifth day of the fifth month move within the Gregorian year and why the seasons of a lunar year do not line up with the seasons of a solar one. Qingming is not one of them: it is named after a division of the solar year, one of the twenty-four, and the divisions are defined by the sun's apparent position, so Qingming arrives on the same date in every year, in early April. That is the diagnostic fact. A festival that visits the dead on a fixed date is a festival attached to a season rather than to a month, and the seasonal explanation is the one to reach for: spring is when the ground can be worked, and the custom of tending a grave requires it. The comparison with a festival set by the lunar calendar is worth keeping in the same breath, because the two together explain the whole of the Chinese festival calendar to a reader. The distractors each assign a calendar basis. B is the mechanism that actually produces shifting dates, and it is the wrong one here. C is the useful thing to rule out, since a fixed date that a government could alter would not be fixed at all. D is close to the truth about the season and wrong about the custom, since the custom is not agricultural even though its timing suits agriculture.
questions.hint: Ask whether this festival's date moves within the Gregorian year, and what fixes the divisions of the solar year.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: Why local gazetteers are valuable
questions.learningObjective: select what a compiled local record is good evidence for
questions.stem: Local gazetteers were compiled under state direction and record a district's geography, products, taxes, schools, bridges and notable people. Four of the five uses below are ones such a record can properly support. Which four?

options.text: Establishing what a district contained and what it produced, since that is exactly what the compiler was required to survey
Tracing the course of local institutions such as schools and temples over several centuries, since gazetteers were revised periodically
Showing what the state thought was worth recording, which is a fact about the priorities of the administration
Comparing what was assessed in tax with what was collected, since the two appear in the same volume and diverge
Establishing how many people lived in the district, since a survey of buildings and bridges is a survey of the population
options.misconception: reads a record of property as a record of people, which is the confusion the item is built to catch

questions.explanation: Gazetteers are a gift to historians for a reason that is worth stating, and the reason is that they were written by officials for administrative purposes, which means they are both detailed and interested. The four keyed uses each follow from that. What a district contained and produced is what a survey was commissioned to find out. The course of local institutions can be traced because the gazetteers were compiled and then revised over centuries, so a reader has a series of snapshots taken by people using a similar method, which is the closest thing to a repeated measurement that the premodern record offers. The priorities of the administration are visible directly, since a compiler recorded what his office cared about, and the silences are as informative as the entries: a district that produces no entry for a particular kind of thing is telling the reader what the state did not track. And the divergence between the tax assessed and the tax collected is a permanent research opportunity, because those two numbers are in the same book and do not match, and the gap is where smuggling, exemption, arrears and under-reporting live. The fifth use is the trap, and it is one of the commonest errors in working with premodern records: a gazetteer is a record of property, institutions and duties, not of people, and a list of bridges tells a reader nothing about how many households a district had. Inferring a population from a property survey is exactly the move that produces confident numbers with no basis.
questions.hint: Ask why an official compiled the volume, and what a record of buildings is not a record of.

questions.learningObjective: describe how a collection and its building are related
questions.stem: The largest collection of the imperial court's objects is housed in a building that was itself the imperial palace, and its galleries are arranged by material rather than by date. What is the best explanation of that arrangement?

The collection was brought together after the dynasty ended, so keeping it in the palace was a way of using an empty building
options.misconception: reverses the direction, since the collection accumulated over the dynasties in use

options.text: Arranging by material is a modern curatorial decision, so the arrangement says more about the museum than about the court that assembled the objects

options.text: The palace was chosen for its size, since the collection was too large for any other building in the capital
options.misconception: reduces the choice to a matter of space and ignores the continuity of institution

When the court stopped and the building became a public museum, the rooms kept their names and the objects stayed where they were, and a catalogue organised by material is simply a description of that inherited arrangement. This is the same principle as the earlier point about institutions outlasting a dynasty, applied to a building and a collection: the survival of a thing is not a decision, it is a residue. A reader who knows this can also read the museum's structure as data, because the gaps are informative. A palace used by a court is a record of what a court did, and it is notably not a record of what ordinary people owned or how they lived, so the museum that grew out of it is strong on ceremony, dress, instruments and objects of office and thin on the material of daily life. C attributes a modern arrangement to modern curators without evidence, which is a common assumption and a bad one when the building explains the layout. D reduces the choice to size, which is the explanation a reader reaches for when the institutional relationship is not considered.

questions.topic: What an official return is a record of
questions.learningObjective: state the scope and the limit of an official administrative record
questions.stem: An official tax register of a district records for every household the amount assessed. Which statement about the register is the most defensible?

options.text: It is a reliable record of what the state assessed and a poor record of what it collected or what was produced, because those are three different numbers
It is a reliable record of what the district actually paid, since the number in the register was collected by the official who wrote it
options.misconception: confuses an assessment with a receipt, which is the confusion the register is best used to expose

options.text: It is a reliable record of the district's wealth, since a state's assessment is a measurement of what a household can bear
options.misconception: treats a fiscal judgement as a measurement, when the two differ whenever a rate is set by policy

options.text: It is unreliable throughout, since an official who collected the tax had a reason to record a smaller total
options.misconception: dismisses a whole class of source, when the register is excellent for exactly the number it was written to hold

questions.explanation: The discipline this item teaches is separating three numbers that a reader is invited to run together. What the state assessed is the figure in the register, and it is a good record of that, because the register exists to hold it and every clerk's interest was in making the total add up. What the district actually paid is a different number, and it is lower than the assessment wherever there was an exemption, an inability to pay, an arrangement with a local collector, or a family that had moved. What the district produced is a third number again, and a large gap between it and the assessment is the normal case: an assessment is a claim about ability, set by a rate fixed in advance by people who were not in the district. Every modern state has this structure and every archive of one does too, which is why the comparison between an assessment and a return is one of the most productive things a reader can do with a tax record. C is the fiscal claim read as a measurement, which is wrong whenever the rate is a policy variable. D is the overcorrection that disqualifies a source because its compiler might have had a motive, and it is worth resisting firmly: a record written by a person with a motive is still a record of what that person wrote down, and what the person wrote down is the number the office needed.
questions.hint: Ask how many different numbers a district can be associated with on a given day, and which of them the register holds.

questions.stem: An account states that a song was composed at a revolutionary base in the 1940s, though the earliest dated record of the song places its composition in the mid-1930s in a different region, and no source from the 1940s places it at the base. Which judgement is soundest?

options.text: The account is a later association, and a reader should say so rather than repeat it, while noticing that the association can be more important than the origin
The account must be correct, since a song sung there for years must have been written there
options.misconception: infers an origin from a later use, which is precisely the inference at issue

options.text: The account and the dated record describe two different songs, so the record has been misfiled
options.misconception: multiplies entities rather than dating a claim, which is the wrong repair

options.text: The dated record must be false, since a contemporary document is more reliable than a later account
options.misconception: applies a rule about one kind of record to another, when a later account can be honest and simply mistaken

questions.explanation: The case is a clean one for teaching the difference between an origin and an association, because both are true and they are about different things. The song was composed where the dated record says, and it was later sung in a place where it became associated with a period and a movement, and the second fact is not a rival to the first: a song travels, and a place can come to claim a song that was written elsewhere, particularly when the song fits what the place wants to remember. The sound judgement is therefore not that the account is false but that it is a later association, and a reader who can say that is doing something useful, because the label keeps the two claims apart. The second half of the keyed answer is the more interesting part, and it should not be skipped: an association can matter more than an origin. A song's presence at a base for years, sung by the people who were there, is a genuine historical fact about that community, and a reader who dismisses the association as an error has thrown away the evidence along with the overstatement. The practical habit is to keep the two in separate columns. Write down what the earliest record shows, write down where the song was later used, and never let the second sentence answer a question the first was asked. D applies a rule about records to a comparison between a record and a later account, and a careful reader will note that the rule it appeals to is not sound, since a contemporary document is evidence about its own time and a later account is evidence about its own time too.
questions.hint: Ask what the earliest record shows, ask where the song was later sung, and keep the two in separate columns.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: A claim the population contradicts
questions.learningObjective: diagnose a claim about a period that the evidence reverses
questions.stem: Stage one: a textbook claim says that after 1949 internal migration was effectively impossible, because a household registration system tied a person to a fixed place. Diagnose why the claim is not supportable. Stage two: say what kind of evidence reverses it, and state what a correct version of the claim would say.

answer.exemplar: Stage one. The claim confuses a legal position with an actual one, and the confusion is the kind that a reader of institutional arrangements makes by default: a rule on paper is treated as a description of conduct. The household registration system did fix a person's registered place, and moving a household registration was a matter of permission rather than of choice, so the legal position is correctly stated. What the claim then does is draw a conclusion about movement, and that conclusion requires something the rule alone does not provide, which is evidence about what millions of people did. It is available. From the early 1980s a very large population left their registered place to work in the cities and the coastal provinces for most of their adult lives, in numbers large enough to be visible in a city's labour force, in its construction sites and in its schools, and the scale is not in doubt even where the precise figures are. So the rule is real and the conclusion is false, and the diagnosis is a specific one: the claim has taken an institutional arrangement and read it as a behavioural fact. That pattern is worth naming as a general hazard in the study of this period, because there is a version of it running in both directions. A claim that a system was wholly permissive is as unsupported as a claim that it was wholly restrictive, and in both cases the reader has taken a document describing a rule and used it to describe a population. Stage two. The evidence that reverses the claim is of several kinds and they are worth distinguishing, because they work differently. Movement that is visible in the record of places: a city whose population grew several times over in a decade did so by migration, and a city is not a fixed number. Movement visible in the record of institutions: schools, housing and transport built for a population that was not there in 1979. Movement visible in administrative practice: the rules themselves had to be amended to accommodate it, which is a signal that was widely known and was widely acted against. And the experiences recorded in the accounts of the migrants themselves, which is a class of source that exists in volume and that a reader should treat with the ordinary critical attention. What a correct version of the claim would say is a version with a subject, a date and a limit: that the registered household of a person stayed fixed through this period, and that the people who worked away from it were outside the system of local benefits that registration controlled, and that this was a large arrangement rather than a formal one. The general lesson is that a claim about a period has to be about what people did inside an arrangement, and that an arrangement, however strict, is a description of paper and a population is a description of conduct. Where the two conflict, the record of conduct is the one that settles what happened.

A response that says the rule was enforced too strictly has answered a different question from the one the diagnosis asked for.
